## Process before Agile

While today the idea of approaching software development in iterative fashion sounds pretty standard, that was not always the case.

In the 90s and early 00s software development was largely viewed as a *sequential* process.

***

The whole project delivery would be split up into distinct phases, and one phase would have to be completed before the next phase could begin.

When thinking visually, this approach, where phases move forward one after another and never backwards, resembles a waterfall, where water only falls down and not up. Thus it was given the *waterfall* name.

::: {.notes}
Historically this was most likely because software engineering being a new field (relatively speaking) did not have standardized practices yet and had to borrow these practices from neighboring fields. Some of these neighboring fields were building construction and hardware manufacturing. When a building is being built, once a 2nd floor is finished, it would be impractical to completely redo the 1st floor, thus it creates a need to plan in advance, because redos might be overly costly. The same applies to computer hardware: because manufacturing is a costly process, it might be too expensive to manufacture multiple chips just to find out that they are not behaving exactly as needed.

However software development has one big difference from these other fields - it is (relatively) cheap to change. Ignoring maintenance, technical debt and similar considerations, it is very easy to change some functionality and deploy it to make it available to all users. Because of this, approaches like thinking of a solution to a problem, developing an iteration of the solution, getting user feedback and adjusting the solution to the given feedback become viable in software engineering, but not necessarily in other fields.
:::

### Waterfall visualized

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    Requirements->>Analysis: Analysis
    Analysis->>Design: Design
    Design->>Coding: Coding
    Coding->>Testing: Testing
    Testing->>Deployment: Deployment
    Deployment->>Maintenance: Maintenance
```

### What Royce actually wrote

The diagram everyone copies comes from Winston Royce, 1970.

::: {.fragment}
Royce called that simple sequential version risky and likely to fail.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The paper argues for building the system twice, with feedback between phases.
:::

::: {.fragment}
The word "waterfall" does not appear in it.
:::

***

"waterfall vs agile" is not a fight between a naive past and an enlightened present. It is a fight between a procurement document and the people doing the work.

## What is Agile?

Agile could be defined as a software development paradigm that focuses on continuous improvement and iterative approaches.

::: {.fragment}
"Paradigm" just means a set of concepts or thought patterns.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Frameworks like Scrum or Kanban exist to put it into practice.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Following a framework is not what makes a team Agile.
:::

::: {.notes}
Being Agile is about the general principles that are followed and how problems are approached, rather than following some specific routines. A team can run every Scrum ceremony perfectly and not be agile in any meaningful sense, if it still takes six months to get a change in front of a user.
:::

## Manifesto for Agile Software Development

Written in February 2001 at Snowbird, Utah, by 17 software engineers.

Published at [agilemanifesto.org](https://agilemanifesto.org/).

::: {.fragment}
They were mostly independent consultants and trainers, each already promoting their own lightweight method - XP, Scrum, Crystal, DSDM, FDD, Pragmatic Programming. The manifesto is what they could all agree on, which is why it is short and vague.
:::

::: {.fragment}
While these principles appear obvious nowadays, they were not obvious at the time when the manifesto was written.
:::

### The four values

| We value | over |
| --- | --- |
| Individuals and interactions | processes and tools |
| Working software | comprehensive documentation |
| Customer collaboration | contract negotiation |
| Responding to change | following a plan |

::: {.fragment}
It is not that the right column is bad per se, but if left vs right are in conflict, the left wins.
:::

### Twelve principles, four themes

::: {.fragment}
Deliver value early and often
:::

::: {.fragment}
Change is normal, not failure
:::

::: {.fragment}
Teams over process
:::

::: {.fragment}
Technical excellence and continuous improvement
:::

***

In other words:

::: {.fragment}
- Ship small and fast
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Get data points early and often
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Learn to act and adjust based on that data
:::

::: {.fragment}
- Keep codebase in such a state that this stays cheap
:::

### Change is normal, not failure

Learning that something doesn't work is also a valuable outcome.

### Technical excellence and improvement

- Practice attention to good code design
- Refactoring when needed

::: {.fragment}
- The opposite of spaghetti code
:::

## Extreme programming

Extreme programming (XP) predates the Agile term by a few years and shares most of its ideas.

Where the manifesto describes general ideas and principles, XP states **practices**.

### Where XP came from

Chrysler C3 payroll project, 1996. Kent Beck, Ward Cunningham, Ron Jeffries.

::: {.fragment}
If code review is good - review constantly (pair programming)
:::

::: {.fragment}
If testing is good - test every change (TDD)
:::

::: {.fragment}
If integration is good - integrate continuously (CI)
:::

::: {.fragment}
Just take the good practices and apply them rigorously.
:::

### Five values

- Communication
- Simplicity
- Feedback
- Courage
- Respect

### Feedback loops

| Loop | Length |
| --- | --- |
| Pair programming | seconds |
| Unit test | minutes |
| Stand-up | one day |
| Acceptance test | days |
| Iteration plan | weeks |
| Release plan | months |

***

Agility is the length of your **shortest** feedback loop.

### The twelve practices

**Fine-scale feedback**: pair programming, planning game, test driven development, whole team

**Continuous process**: continuous integration, design improvement (refactoring), small releases

**Shared understanding**: coding standard, collective code ownership, simple design, system metaphor

**Programmer welfare**: sustainable pace

### Pair programming: the evidence

- Williams & Kessler, 2000 - ~15% more effort, ~15% fewer defects
- Arisholm et al., 2007 (84 professionals) - effort up sharply; gains concentrated in **complex tasks** and **junior developers**
- Hannay et al., 2009 (meta-analysis) - small quality gain, real effort cost

::: {.fragment}
A review and training tool. Not a free lunch.
:::

### Test driven development: the evidence

- Nagappan et al., 2008 - Microsoft and IBM teams: 40–90% lower defect density, 15–35% more development time

### Continuous integration and small releases

- XP, 1999 - integrate at least daily

::: {.fragment}
- Amazon, 2011 - a deployment every 11.6 seconds on average
:::

### Collective ownership and coding standard

Anyone may change any file.

::: {.fragment}
Which only works with a shared standard, tests, and review.
:::

::: {.fragment}
This is why pull requests exist.
:::

### XP technically won, but practically disappeared

Continuous integration, automated tests, refactoring, small releases, code review.

::: {.fragment}
Today: defaults. Nobody calls them XP.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Agile won the naming battle.
:::

## Scrum

The most used Agile framework - and the one most often blamed.

Scrum adds to the Agile idea:

- **Roles**: product owner, scrum master, developers
- **Events**: sprint planning, daily scrum, sprint review, retrospective
- **Artifacts**: product backlog, sprint backlog, increment

::: {.fragment}
Scrum is deliberately a management framework: it says nothing about how to write code.
:::

### Scrum poster

Scrum.org has a [poster](https://www.scrum.org/resources/scrum-framework-poster) illustrating the process.

### How common is it, really

Digital.ai *18th State of Agile Report*, 2025:

::: {.fragment}
**63%** use Scrum at team level
:::

::: {.fragment}
**74%** use a hybrid, blended or homegrown process
:::

::: {.fragment}
*A bit biased report though.*
:::

## Agile sprints visualized

Sprint is a Scrum term, but it illustrates the Agile loop well: work happens in small batches, and detailed planning covers only the immediate work.

```{mermaid}
graph LR
    A[Product backlog] --> R[Refinement]
    R --> B[Sprint planning]
    B --> C[Sprint]
    C --> D[Daily stand-up]
    D --> C
    C --> E[Increment]
    E --> F[Review]
    F --> G[Retrospective]
    G --> A
```

### Backlog

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Purpose** | one ordered list of everything that might be built |
| **Looks like** | user stories, ordered by value, coarse at the bottom |
| **Artifact** | GitHub issues, labelled, ordered in a project board |
| **Failure mode** | issues titled "frontend stuff" |


::: {.fragment}

User story template:

`As a <role>, I want to <feature>, so that <benefit>.`
:::

::: {.fragment}
`As a commuter, I want to search for routes, so that I can pick the best way to get to my destination.`
:::

### Refinement

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Purpose** | make the top of the backlog ready before planning |
| **Looks like** | splitting, clarifying, adding acceptance criteria |
| **Artifact** | issues with checklists, linked to a parent issue |
| **Failure mode** | refinement discovered mid-sprint |

::: {.fragment}
Rule of thumb: an issue nobody can finish in a day is not one issue.

Artifact: an issue that is detailed enough to be picked up and completed within a day.
:::

### Sprint planning

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Purpose** | commit to a goal, not to a pile of tickets |
| **Looks like** | one sentence goal, then issues chosen to serve it |
| **Artifact** | a milestone named `Sprint 3` whose description is the goal |
| **Failure mode** | pulling in everything, finishing nothing |

::: {.fragment}
Sprint 3: a guest can join a room by link and see the current question
:::

### Definition of Done

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Purpose** | one shared meaning of "finished" |
| **Looks like** | a short checklist every change must satisfy |
| **Artifact** | `docs/definition-of-done.md`, mirrored in the PR template |
| **Failure mode** | "done" meaning "works on my machine" |

::: {.fragment}
>Reviewed + tested + merged to main + deployed + documented
:::

### Daily stand-up

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Purpose** | re-plan the day, surface blockers |
| **Looks like** | 10 minutes, walking the board right to left |
| **Artifact** | board state that changes daily, blockers as issue comments |
| **Failure mode** | three ritual questions reported "what I did yesterday, what I will do today, what is blocking me" |

### Increment

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Purpose** | produce something a user could actually use |
| **Looks like** | end-to-end and deployed, however thin |
| **Artifact** | a new release, a git tag, as per your definition of done |
| **Failure mode** | three finished layers that have never met |

::: {.fragment}
**Walking skeleton**: the thinnest end-to-end slice that runs in production.
:::

### Review

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Purpose** | get feedback from outside the team |
| **Looks like** | a demo of the deployed system, by a **user** path |
| **Artifact** | a closed milestone, plus notes on the feedback and resulting changes |
| **Failure mode** | slides about the app instead of the app |

### Retrospective

| | |
| --- | --- |
| **Purpose** | improve the process, not the product |
| **Looks like** | 30 minutes, everyone speaks, the past sprint only |
| **Artifact** | `docs/retros/sprint-03.md` and **one** action item with an owner |
| **Failure mode** | complaints with no owner, repeated every sprint |

### Artifacts in your project

- Issues as user stories, ordered
- A milestone per sprint, with a goal in its description
- `docs/definition-of-done.md` + PR template
- Defined increments in some way
- `docs/retros/sprint-NN.md` + one `retro-action` issue each sprint

## Kanban and flow

Work is visualized as items moving through fixed stages.

```text
+----------------+--------------------+----------------+
|    To Do       |  In Progress (2)   |     Done       |
+----------------+--------------------+----------------+
| - Task 1       | - Task 4           | - Task 7       |
| - Task 2       | - Task 5           | - Task 8       |
| - Task 3       |                    | - Task 9       |
+----------------+--------------------+----------------+
```

The number in the column header is a **WIP limit**

## Estimation

- **Story points** - relative size, not hours
- **Planning poker** - estimate simultaneously, discuss the disagreements
- **Velocity** - points finished per sprint, used as capacity

### The cone of uncertainty

Estimates at the start of a project are off by a large factor in **both** directions.

::: {.fragment}
The cone narrows by building, not by planning harder.
:::

### Or: skip the estimates

Fix the time, vary the scope.

::: {.fragment}
Basecamp's Shape Up: set fixed time cycle, start cutting the scope to fit.
:::

## Agile in the industry

Nobody runs the textbook.

### Agile criticism

Even done "*correctly*", the approach has recurring problems:

- **Unpredictability** - delivery dates are hard to forecast, while the business still needs them
- **Scope creep** - a vaguely understood scope lets features slide in
- **Documentation** - what is skipped is rarely written later
- **Client inclusion** - quick, reliable customer feedback is easier said than done

***

The "agile projects succeed 3x more often" figure comes from the Standish CHAOS reports.

::: {.fragment}
Eveleens & Verhoef, 2010: the methodology does not support the claim.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Most numbers in this field are produced by someone selling something.
:::

### The critics are the authors

- Dave Thomas, 2015 - *Agile is Dead (Long Live Agility)*
- Ron Jeffries, 2018 - *Developers Should Abandon Agile*
- Martin Fowler, 2018 - the *Agile Industrial Complex*

***

There is no correct process. There is a process that fits the risk.

::: {.fragment}
In practice: 74% hybrid.
:::
